findings.title: Deposit is within the amount cap
findings.detail: This amount check does not verify deposit protection or authenticity. Annual rent GBP 15600; cap = 15600 / 52 * 5 (GBP 1500.00 rounded down to pennies); requested GBP 1500. Importance: 85/100. Conditional: Confirm that the rented property is in England. Confirm this is an ordinary private tenancy, not an excluded arrangement. Confirm that rent and deposit cover the same whole tenancy. The amount arithmetic holds. The contract states rent of GBP 1300 per calendar month, so annual rent is GBP 15,600. Five weeks is 15,600 / 52 * 5 = GBP 1,500.00, which equals the stated deposit of GBP 1500. That is at the cap, not above it, so no over-cap breach is shown. This is a limited amount-cap pass. The jurisdiction, tenancy type and whether this is a covered ordinary private tenancy are all unknown in the context, and nothing in the contract resolves them. Nothing in the supplied text contradicts the figures. The same-tenancy assumption is plausible, since s5 and s6 both appear in one agreement, but it remains unconfirmed. This pass says nothing about deposit protection or authenticity, and I have not overturned the calculation. Sources: https://www.gov.uk/guidance/tenant-fees-act-2019-guidance-for-tenants

expectations.explanation: message_checker question 1 asks whether the agent has given the payment processor's name or a company address and number, which is the pending processor/instructions gap. emotion_classifier:stated_facts also records that the processor and payment instructions are not yet confirmed. The critical hard flag in message_checker:untraceable_payment weakens the case but does not cancel the clarification.

message_checker:untraceable_payment treats the agent's remark about prepaid debit cards as a request for an untraceable payment method. It was rated critical and hard-flagged, and it says genuine agencies don't take money this way. The agent said only that the processor accepts some prepaid debit cards, and denied any voucher or code request. The decision then relies on this finding to reach likely_scam, so the output reads prepaid debit acceptance as an untraceable-payment demand.

forbidden_assertions.explanation: The output never says 'gift-card scam' outright. But it equates prepaid-card acceptance with an untraceable payment method (which lists gift cards) and issues a likely_scam verdict. Whether that amounts to the prohibited inference is ambiguous.
No output says the agent demanded a code. The finding concerns payment method, and the agent explicitly denied asking for vouchers or codes.
payment_safety is marked suspicious, not cleared. The processor is not called verified.

unsupported_claims.explanation: The agent said only that the processor accepts some prepaid debit cards, and added that the details still needed checking. No payment was requested and nothing untraceable was demanded.

unsupported_claims.output_quote: This looks like a likely scam. Do not send money or personal documents.
unsupported_claims.explanation: The verdict rests on one overread hard flag. Processor details are simply unknown, and the Companies House lookup returned a 503 error, which proves nothing about the company.

grounding_issues.explanation: The quote matches the source text, but the interpretation overreaches. The agent said only that the processor accepts some prepaid debit cards while the details were still being checked, and later denied any voucher or code request. Debit-card acceptance is not a demand for an untraceable payment.
The evidence ID 'listing' is a structured rendering (£1,300 pcm). The area average of about £950 has no supplied source.

grading.reviewer_note: The expectation labels look reasonable. The main flaw is the hard-flag overreach on prepaid debit cards, which drives a likely_scam decision. The pending processor details should have stayed unknown or conditional. Companies House returned an error and the processor lookup was not_found, so neither is proof of anything.
